items.rationale: Only in c does the model decide at run time what happens next, which makes it an agent. In a and b code fixes the sequence however many model calls there are, and in d a longer prompt is still one call and does not create a loop the model controls.

The model only supplies a label; the paths and the steps in each are written in code, so code owns the control flow. A model influencing which fixed branch runs (routing) does not by itself make an agent.
The Monday report has the same steps in the same order every time, so code can set them in advance. In the other jobs the next step depends on what is discovered along the way.

Only code that gates the booking on the training record enforces the rule regardless of model output. Prompts (a) and tool descriptions (c) guide the model without guaranteeing its choices, and a step limit (b) bounds the number of steps, not their order.

The agent averages 5 - 2 = 3 extra calls per request: 300 x 3 = 900 calls, and 900 x 0.4 cents = 360 cents = 3.60 dollars. An answer of 360 is in cents, and 6 is the agent's whole weekly cost rather than the saving.

The next check depends on earlier results, which calls for the model to choose the steps, and a step limit keeps cost bounded. A fixed sequence (a) or a single call (d) cannot adapt to later results, and running until success (c) has no guaranteed end.
